column1: Why can't translation be represented as a pure linear (matrix) transformation in 3D Cartesian coordinates, and how do homogeneous coordinates fix this?
column2: Translation adds a constant offset, breaking the closure property of linear operators (linear maps must fix the origin). Homogeneous coordinates embed 3D points as 4D vectors (x,y,z,1), allowing translation to be encoded as matrix multiplication alongside rotation/scaling, unifying all affine transforms into one 4x4 matrix operation.

column1: In homogeneous coordinates, how are points and vectors (directions) distinguished?
column2: By the w-component: points use w=1 (e.g., (x,y,z,1)), while vectors/directions use w=0 (e.g., (x,y,z,0)), since directions have no position and should be unaffected by translation.

column1: List the five major coordinate spaces a vertex passes through in the rendering pipeline, in order.
column2: Object space → World space → View (camera) space → Clip space (post-projection) → Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) / screen space.

column1: Why is profiling a GPU rendering pipeline fundamentally different from general systems profiling?
column2: The pipeline is a producer-consumer graph with fixed throughput stages (vertex shading, primitive assembly, rasterization, fragment shading); overall performance is limited by the slowest stage's throughput (the bottleneck), not by finding the single slowest function call as in traditional profiling.

column1: What is the key architectural difference between fixed-function and programmable GPU pipeline stages?
column2: Fixed-function stages are implemented in hardwired silicon with a single fixed behavior (e.g., early hardwired vertex transforms or bilinear filtering). Programmable stages are small SIMD shader cores executing user-written programs (GLSL/HLSL/MSL/SPIR-V), enabling custom per-vertex/per-fragment logic.

column1: Name the three major paradigms of geometric representation in graphics and give one defining trait of each.
column2: 1) Boundary representation (B-rep, e.g., triangle meshes) — describes a solid via its enclosing surface. 2) Implicit representation — describes a solid via f(x) ≤ 0, cheap inside/outside tests. 3) Parametric representation — surface as a map S(u,v): R²→R³, natural for splines/NURBS, good for curvature/arc-length.

column1: Why is extracting a triangle mesh from an implicit surface computationally expensive?
column2: It requires a marching cubes pass over a volumetric grid, which is O(N³) in grid resolution, even though evaluating inside/outside membership on the implicit function itself is O(1).

column1: What is the BRDF and what physical invariant must it satisfy?
column2: The Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function f_r(ω_i, ω_o) gives the ratio of outgoing radiance in direction ω_o to incoming irradiance from ω_i. Energy conservation requires the BRDF's integral over the outgoing hemisphere not exceed unity — a surface cannot reflect more light than it receives.

column1: What key substitution differentiates Blinn-Phong from the original Phong reflection model, and why was it introduced?
column2: Blinn-Phong uses the halfway vector (between light and view directions) instead of the explicit mirror reflection vector used by Phong, improving numerical stability and better approximating microfacet behavior at glancing angles.

column1: What are the three multiplicative terms of the Cook-Torrance microfacet BRDF, and what does each model?
column2: D(ω_h) — Normal Distribution Function, statistics of microfacet orientation; G(ω_i, ω_o) — Geometric attenuation term, accounting for facet self-shadowing/masking; F(ω_i, ω_h) — Fresnel term, fraction of light reflected vs. refracted at each microfacet.

column1: What is the foundational invariant that texture mapping exploits, and what signal-processing problem does it introduce?
column2: It decouples sampling rate (texture resolution) from geometric resolution (mesh density), letting artists control each independently. This introduces aliasing: because surface-to-texture projection distorts distances/angles anisotropically, varying minification/magnification across a surface causes shimmering and Moiré artifacts under naive point sampling.

column1: Why have Bounding Volume Hierarchies (BVHs) become the industry-standard ray tracing acceleration structure over uniform grids and k-d trees?
column2: BVHs organize primitives (not space) into nested AABBs, giving robust performance across non-uniform scene distributions. Uniform grids waste memory on non-uniform density scenes; k-d trees/octrees add branching overhead and struggle with primitives straddling partition boundaries. BVHs reduce ray-primitive tests from O(m) toward O(log m) without these pathologies.
